user.text: Create a server component that displays a welcome message and logs the page view to an analytics service. The logging should NOT block the response - use Next.js's recommended approach for scheduling work after the response is sent.

history.assistant:
I added a welcome page that logs each page view to an analytics service after the response has been sent, using `after()` from `next/server`. The bundled Next.js 16 docs name this as the way to run logging and analytics without blocking the response. A build and a test request both worked. **Changes:** - **`app/lib/analytics.ts`** (new): `logPageView()` sends a `page_view` event to the URL in `ANALYTICS_ENDPOINT`. If that isn't set, it prints the event to the console instead. Errors are caught and logged, so a failed analytics call can't break the page. - **`app/page.tsx`**: now shows the welcome message and calls `after()` to log the view. It reads the `user-agent` and `referer` headers while the page renders and passes them into the callback. That's required because Server Components can't call `headers()` or `cookies()` inside `after()`. Reading headers also makes `/` render on every request (`ƒ` in the build output). Without that, `after()` on a static page would only run at build time, so real visits wouldn't be logged. **Checks:** - `npx next build`: passed (exit code 0), with `/` shown as `ƒ (Dynamic)`. - `next start` plus `curl -A test-agent http://localhost:3123/`: the response contained `

Welcome

`, and the server then logged `[analytics] page view { path: '/', userAgent: 'test-agent', referrer: null, ... }`. The shell reported signal 15 at the end because `pkill` stopped the test server, not because the check failed. The build also changed `tsconfig.json` on its own: it set `jsx` to `react-jsx` and added `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts` to `include`. I haven't sent events to a real analytics endpoint; to do that, set `ANALYTICS_ENDPOINT`.

title: after
description: API Reference for the after function.
---

`after` allows you to schedule work to be executed after a response (or prerender) is finished. This is useful for tasks and other side effects that should not block the response, such as logging and analytics.

It can be used in [Server Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components) (including [`generateMetadata`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata)), [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy).

The function accepts a callback that will be executed after the response (or prerender) is finished:

```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
import { after } from 'next/server'
// Custom logging function
import { log } from '@/app/utils'

export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  after(() => {
    // Execute after the layout is rendered and sent to the user
    log()
  })
  return <>{children}</>
}
```

```jsx filename="app/layout.jsx" switcher
import { after } from 'next/server'
// Custom logging function
import { log } from '@/app/utils'

export default function Layout({ children }) {
  after(() => {
    // Execute after the layout is rendered and sent to the user
    log()
  })
  return <>{children}</>
}
```

> **Good to know:** `after` is not a [Request-time API](/docs/app/glossary#request-time-apis) and calling it does not cause a route to become dynamic. If it's used within a static page, the callback will execute at build time, or whenever a page is revalidated.

## Reference

### Parameters

- A callback function which will be executed after the response (or prerender) is finished.

### Duration

`after` will run for the platform's default or configured max duration of your route. If your platform supports it, you can configure the timeout limit using the [`maxDuration`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/maxDuration) route segment config.

## Good to know

- `after` will be executed even if the response didn't complete successfully. Including when an error is thrown or when `notFound` or `redirect` is called.
- In Server Components, you can use React [`cache`](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) to deduplicate functions called inside `after`. The callback reuses values already computed during the render. See [Reusing data with `React.cache`](/docs/app/getting-started/fetching-data#reusing-data-with-reactcache).
- `after` can be nested inside other `after` calls, for example, you can create utility functions that wrap `after` calls to add additional functionality.

## Examples

### With request APIs

Whether you can use request APIs like [`cookies`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) and [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers) inside `after` depends on where `after` is called from.

#### In Route Handlers and Server Functions

You can call `cookies` and `headers` directly inside the `after` callback when used in [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) and [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data). This is useful for logging activity after a mutation or API request. For example:

import { cookies, headers } from 'next/headers'
import { logUserAction } from '@/app/utils'

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  // Perform mutation
  // ...
